Your instinct is right, and I'll give it to you straight: there is no rounding that turns 3 failures into 0. What you're looking at is either an undocumented re-run (sloppy) or falsification of a controlled quality record (serious). Either way, the response is the same, and the good news is that the safest path for you and the right path for patients converge — but only if you act quietly and in the right order this week.

**The reframe that matters:** your job here is not to single-handedly stop the shipment or confront anyone as a fraud. Your job is to trigger the process your company already has. Every ISO 13485 medical-device company has a nonconformance (NC) procedure for exactly this. "3 units failed, the report says they didn't" *is* a nonconformance. Framing it that way makes you procedural instead of heroic — and procedural is what keeps people employed.

**The plan, in order:**

1. **Preserve evidence today, quietly.** Save the original report version (3/40 fail), the changed version, revision numbers, dates, any email about the change, and file metadata if visible. Write a dated, signed memo of your conversation with your boss: who said what, when, in what words. Store copies off company systems (personal encrypted storage, printout at home). Keep the set minimal — evidence of the discrepancy, not the whole technical file.

2. **Do not sign the false version.** If you haven't signed yet, that's your leverage and your shield. If the report was altered after your sign-off, the QMS revision history will show it — and your written objection becomes critical. Either way, your name never goes on a record that contradicts the raw data. This is non-negotiable, and it's also what protects *you*: if a patient is ever harmed, investigators will find that the original report existed, and the question becomes who flagged it. You want to be that person, on paper, dated before the ship date.

3. **Send one boring, factual email to your boss.** Something like:

   > *"Hi [Boss], following up on the low-battery alarm report. The current version shows 40/40 pass, but the raw data from run [X] shows 3 failures out of 40. I can't reconcile that with rounding, so before this goes into the design history file I'd like to open an NC and get the discrepancy documented. If it turns out to be a fixture or setup artifact, we note that and keep the timeline — a 3-unit alarm investigation and targeted retest is days, not months. Can we book 30 min with QA this week?"*

   No words like "fraud," "regulator," or "whistleblower." Those burn your off-ramp and can even be twisted into threats. Stay boring. Boring emails survive audits and lawsuits.

4. **Actually investigate the failures.** Check whether the 3 units cluster — same serial range, same test fixture channel, same run. If it's a test-setup artifact, a verified retest of those 3 units can resolve this properly within a week, and the product still ships with true records. This makes you the person solving the problem, not blocking it.

5. **If your boss stonewalls, go to QA/RA directly.** In a med-device company, Quality owns these records and may not know what happened. "I raised this with [boss] on [date] and want to make sure the NC gets opened" is a completely normal thing to say to a QA manager. If your company has an internal ethics line — or a parent company's hotline, common if it's a subsidiary of a US or EU group — that's another internal channel.

6. **Get a one-hour consult with a Swiss employment lawyer early**, before any escalation, not after. CHF 200–300 against your entire livelihood and visa is cheap. Check whether you have private legal-expenses insurance (Rechtsschutzversicherung) — many Swiss households do, and it often covers employment disputes. The lawyer can also tell you how to frame a report to Swissmedic if it comes to that.

**Escalation ladder if internal channels fail:** QA head → ethics/compliance hotline → lawyer → written report to Swissmedic *before the ship date*. Swiss courts' case law on whistleblowing generally expects internal channels first and proportionate disclosure, so this sequence also builds your legal position. Don't skip to the top unless the ship date is imminent and the false report is still intact.

**About the visa — the honest math:**

- **Do not resign.** This is the single most important sentence here. Quitting likely forfeits Swiss unemployment benefits (ALV) and looks voluntary to the migration office. If you're dismissed, you get your statutory notice period (1–3 months depending on tenure, 7 days if in probation), ALV eligibility, and — for tied permits — usually a grace period to find a new job while receiving benefits. Confirm specifics for your permit type and canton with the lawyer.
- Junior test engineers with IEC 62304 / ISO 13485 exposure are employable in Basel, Zurich, Zug, Lausanne. "I identified a falsified test record and escalated it through proper channels, in writing" is a survivable story in this industry — *if* your paper trail shows you were procedural rather than dramatic. That's another reason for the boring email.
- Your real personal risk runs the other direction. Falsified technical documentation on a life-sustaining device is a criminal matter in Switzerland, and far more so if a pump shuts down silently on a user. Silence isn't the safe option; it just relocates the risk onto you.

**What not to do:** don't resign in the heat of the moment; don't fix or annotate the report yourself; don't threaten regulators in writing; don't broadcast to colleagues beyond one trusted witness if you have one; don't post anything identifiable online.

You're not overreacting, and your fear is rational — but this is a workable situation, and a low-battery alarm failing on 7.5% of units is fixable if someone with your paper trail forces the question now, four weeks before shipping.

If you tell me three things — whether you've signed the current report, whether it lives in an eQMS with revision history, and whether your permit is EU/EFTA or third-country — I can help you draft the NC text and the exact email wording.

Also: if they're EU/EFTA national, permit is less fragile (they get B permit tied to employment but easier to switch). The person didn't specify. This reframing is useful: the ask isn't "delay the product forever," it's "follow the process you already have." That gives the boss a face-saving off-ramp and gives the engineer a professional, non-heroic script. One nuance: the person says "test report... changed." I should ask/consider: is the change in the controlled eQMS or a local file? And did they find the old version (so evidence exists)? They noticed it, so they have some access. Advise: capture the old version now, before it's overwritten further; note revision history.

Also the phrase "make noise": reframe — the goal is to make *records*, not noise. Quiet, procedural, written. Noise is what gets people fired; paper is what protects them and fixes the problem. That's a nice memorable line: "Don't make noise; make a paper trail. Paper is louder in the end."

Scripts — draft:

To boss (email, short, neutral):
"Hi [Boss], following up on the low-battery alarm report. The released version shows 40/40 pass, but test run [X] raw data shows 3 failures out of 40. I can't reconcile that as a rounding issue, so before the report goes into the DHF I'd like to open an NC and get the discrepancy documented — if it turns out to be a fixture/setup artifact, we can note that and keep the ship date. Can we book 30 minutes this week with QA?"

To QA (if boss stonewalls): similar, plus "I raised this with [boss] on [date]; attaching what I have."

If pressured verbally: "I hear you on the date. My constraint is simple: I can't put my name on a report that doesn't match the raw data. If we open the NC today, investigation and retest can still fit the timeline."

If asked to sign the false version: "I'll sign once the report matches the data or the NC documents the justification."

Escalation ladder, explicitly: manager → QA/RA head → (if exists) internal ethics/compliance hotline or parent-company hotline → lawyer → Swissmedic (before ship date). Add: at any point they may skip to lawyer; and if ship date imminent with false report intact, external report is justified; do it in writing, keep evidence.

Job/visa reality section:
- Do not resign. Dismissal ≠ resignation for ALV and permit purposes.
- Even if dismissed: 1–3 months' notice + ALV + permit grace period usually; med-device QA/test skills are in demand in CH (Basel, Zug, Zurich, Lausanne clusters). A junior test engineer with 13485/62304 exposure gets interviews.
- The narrative "I flagged a falsified test report through proper channels" is survivable and even valued in this industry — IF it's documented as professional and procedural, not as a dramatic confrontation. Another reason for the boring-email approach.
- Get the legal consult before any external step; bring the memo and copies.
- Check legal-expenses insurance; some unions/associations help.

What not to do:
- Don't alter or "fix" the report themselves; don't sign; don't email the raw data file around; don't accuse fraud in writing early; don't threaten regulators; don't post on LinkedIn/Reddit with identifying details; don't take the whole technical file; don't discuss with colleagues broadly (choose confidants carefully; word travels).

Also small practical: back up the memo and screenshots outside company systems, and keep contemporaneous diary entries going forward (date-stamped).

Mention: if the company is part of a US-listed parent or sells in US, FDA's rules make this worse for the company; leverage point in the internal conversation: "This gets caught at the notified body audit / FDA inspection; better it's an NC now than an FDA 483 later." Hmm, careful: mentioning FDA in the email is fine as process logic, not threat. Maybe keep that line out of scripts but mention as leverage verbally.

Also: the 3 failed units — suggest checking whether failures cluster (same serial range? same fixture channel?). If it's a fixture artifact, a targeted retest of the 3 units on a verified fixture may resolve it within days. This is constructive, shows them a path to "product ships and records are true," and gives them a concrete engineering contribution that builds goodwill rather than adversarial posture. I like including this because actual advice for a junior test engineer includes the engineering: investigate root cause, don't just litigate the report.

One more: who else knows? If a colleague co-signed or saw the original, quietly confirm. Witnesses matter. But be discreet — one trusted colleague, not a campaign.

Length check: I want this comprehensive but readable. Use headers + numbered steps + two short scripts. Maybe ~800–1000 words. The stakes justify it. Avoid excessive statute citation; keep 2–3 concrete Swiss facts with hedges.

Opening: no fluff. Start with the bottom line: "You don't have to choose between your visa and a clean report today — but you do have to act this week, and the first moves are quiet ones." Something like that. Then structure.

Also, address the emotional layer briefly: the fear is rational, the situation is genuinely hard, they're not overreacting — one sentence, not therapy.

Let me also decide: should I say "this is likely falsification and it's a criminal matter"? Yes, plainly but without melodrama, because it justifies both urgency and their instinct, and because their personal exposure depends on knowing that silence isn't neutral. Phrase: "There is no rounding that turns 3 failures into 0. What happened is either a sloppy undocumented re-run or falsification of a controlled record. Either way, the fix is the same: documented investigation. And if it's the latter, the people who changed the record — not you — carry the exposure, provided your name isn't on the false version."

Personal exposure point: they may already be named on the original report as author. If the report was edited after release, metadata/QMS history shows it. Their defense is having raised it in writing. Emphasize.

Swissmedic contact: I believe Swissmedic has a general contact and a vigilance office; there's also a reporting portal for incidents. For suspected illegal activity, writing to Swissmedic (or the cantonal authority?) — devices are federal. Keep generic: "a written report to Swissmedic; a lawyer can help frame it and advise on anonymity."

Finally, offer follow-up help: "If you tell me whether you've signed the report, whether it's in an eQMS with revision history, and whether your permit is EU/EFTA or third-country, I can help you draft the NC text and the email." That invites the practical continuation.
